```{r}
# Set seed
set.seed(3)
```


## Problem 1

Suppose I recruit a sample of $n$ teachers to study the effect of hydration and sleep
on voice quality. Define the following variables:

- $H_i$ is the harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) of the $i$th participant's voice.
This is a measure of voice quality and is measured in decibels.
- $S_i = 1$ if participant $i$ slept well the night before they were assessed and
$S_i = 0$ if they slept poorly.
- $W_i$ is the number of liters of water the $i$th participant drank in
the previous 24 hours.

Suppose I fit the following model:
$$
H_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \beta_2 W_i + \epsilon_i \text{.}
$$
Please answer the following questions,
assuming all necessary assumptions are met.

### Part (a)

(4 points)
What does $\beta_0$ mean in real-world terms?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
HNR (1 point) for a teacher who slept poorly the night before (1 point)
and drank no water (1 point) in the past 24 hours.

:::

### Part (b)

What does $\beta_1$ mean in real-world terms?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
difference (1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
between those who slept well (1 point)
and those who slept poorly (1 point),
holding water consumption constant (or "all else constant"; 1 point).

:::

### Part (c)

What does $\beta_2$ mean in real-world terms?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
change (or increase; 1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
associated with a one-liter increase (1 point)
in water consumption (1 point),
holding sleep quality constant (1 point).

Alternatively,
the expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
difference (1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
between two populations of teachers
that differ by one liter (1 point)
in their water consumption (1 point)
but had the same sleep quality (1 point).

:::

## Problem 2

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Scatter plot of the residuals against the fitted values for a multiple linear regression."
# Set parameter values
n <- 1e4

# Generate data
x <- rnorm(n = n)
y <- rnorm(n = n)

# Plot
plot(x = x,
     y = y,
     xlab = "Fitted values",
     ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")
```

Suppose @fig-scatter contains a scatter plot of the residuals against the fitted values
for a multiple linear regression.
For each assumption below, do the following:

- State whether @fig-scatter is evidence for the validity
of the assumption in this data set, evidence against it,
or provides no information.
- If you decide that @fig-scatter is evidence for or against the assumption,
justify your decision.
If you decide that @fig-scatter provides no information about the assumption,
state what would be informative instead.


### Part (a)

(2 points)
$E(\epsilon_i|$all the $X_{ij}$'s$) = 0$

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-scatter is evidence for the validity of this assumption
in this data set.
The reference line goes right through the center of the cloud of points.
In other words, if we chose any fitted value and averaged the residuals nearby,
the result would be approximately zero.

:::

### Part (b)

(2 points)
The observations are iid.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-scatter provides no information.
Instead, we would need to examine how the data were collected.

:::

### Part (c)

(2 points)
$Var(\epsilon_i|$all the $X_{ij}$'s$) = \sigma^2$

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-scatter is evidence for the validity of this assumption
in this data set.
The vertical spread of the residuals is approximately the same
for every fitted value.

:::

### Part (d)

(2 points)
$\epsilon_i$ is normally distributed,
conditional on all the $X_{ij}$'s.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-scatter provides no information.
In order to evaluate this assumption,
we would need to look at a histogram and/or Q-Q plot.

:::

## Problem 3

(4 points)
Suppose you and your colleagues agree that the following assumptions are met for 
a multiple linear regression that you've run:

- $E(\epsilon_i|\text{all the $X_{ij}$'s}) = 0$.

Without any additional information,
which of the following claims can you make?
Select all that apply.

(a) We can interpret the coefficients.
(b) The standard errors are accurate.
(c) If we increase our sample size, our estimators will get close to the true values.
(d) We can interpret the p-values generated by R.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a)

:::
